newsitem.title: UK: Dlr ends little changed in Europe after Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends little changed in Europe after Greenspan.

text.p: The dollar closed little changed in Europe, underpinned by upbeat comments from Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan but unable to build on gains made after his speech.
A recovery of the mark on its European crosses weighed on the dollar's upside, capping it well below the highs of above 1.63 marks and 118 yen hit on Monday, traders said.

Greenspan, in prepared testimony to the Senate budget committee, said U.S. inflation was slower and growth faster than official data suggested. He warned of the risks of wage-driven inflation in the future.

"A lot of excitement had been built into Greenspan's comments before they were made - what he actually said was very much on the lines of what a prudent central banker would say," said Teis Knuthsen, international economist at First Chicago.
The most hawkish comment in Greenspan's speech was the warning on future wage-inflation risks, said Knuthsen.
"His comments still fit very much into the picture of a central bank with a bias to tighten (monetary policy) but in no desperate need to do so," he said.
At 1605 GMT the dollar was at 1.6248/58 marks and 117.85/95 versus 1.6251/56 and 118.03/08 in late Europe on Monday.
Greenspan's speech had been eagerly awaited, in particular after he spooked traders in early December by saying that U.S. asset markets were behaving with "irrational exuberance".
A rebound in U.S. Treasuries from pre-Greenspan lows also helped the dollar a touch higher, traders said.
But as the mark fought back successfully on its European crosses after a recent slide, further dollar/mark gains were hard to come by.
Dollar/yen was sidelined in the European session after conflicting comments overnight from Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzaka and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
Hashimoto sparked a bout of dollar short-covering when he contradicted Mitsuzuka's earlier remarks by saying that the yen's weakness was not excessive.
New York Federal President William McDonough's support for the U.S. government's strong dollar stance also helped to move the dollar off its lows against the yen.

Despite some corrective down-pressure on the dollar, the underlying sentiment remained bullish. Many economist have upgraded their dollar forecasts lately. UBS in London, for example, now expects a dollar rally to 1.75 mark by mid-year, with dollar/yen rising to 125 yen and sterling/mark to 2.80.
"What we're seeing at present is a consolidation on the dollar but the bullish outlook is unchanged," said a senior trader at a German bank.
A rosy economic outlook for the U.S., combined with weak growth expectations in Germany, are likely to continue pushing the dollar higher.

Another hint at German economic weakness came from Germany's Ifo institute today. Its west German business climate index fell to 95.8 in December from 96.9 in November, well below forecasts. Some said this would increase pressure on the Bundesbank to cut interest rates further but few expect a cut soon.
A Reuter poll of ten economists said only one expected a cut in official rates at Thursday's Bundesbank council meeting. All ten forecast another fixed rate repo tender at 3.00 percent.

The pound confounded mark strength on the crosses by rising to a fresh 52-month high at 2.7102 marks. Bank of England Governor Eddie George gave a stern warning late on Monday of the danger of allowing a strong pound to delay a rate rise.

The Confederation of British Industry, however, indicated in its quarterly industrial trends survey that sterling's strong performance smothered cost pressures in manufacturing and exporting. -- Astrid Zweynert London newsroom + 44 171 542 7792
